text: To get a teardown/recreate race, force the activity to be destroyed instead of relying on timing. First check the activity's configChanges in the manifest. If it declares none, rotating to landscape or turning on dark mode destroys and recreates the activity. That also tears down the preview surface and the native engine. This is faster and more reliable than timing a backgrounding against async w

Before you write a real-tap repro, run a direct engine-call replay. Destroy the player, sleep about 500 ms, create the player again if needed, then make a call that comes after the teardown. For a crash in a per-clip engine query, query a clip id the new engine does not have. These replays reached the field frames in about 1–2 minutes, and in one case hit every field frame.

Fire triggers and judge checkpoints from engine log lines, not from fixed delays or UI events. Arm the replay on a when_log line, for example when a converted clip reaches the engine or when the engine destructor message prints. Then right away fire the lifecycle action (home, rotate), or tap the next screen that still calls the engine. A fixed delay only hits some of the time.

Never guess which UI action sends an engine message, and never guess selectors or control positions. Find in the code which confirmed UI action actually sends the expected engine message, and script exactly that action. Opening and leaving a tool is often not enough, because the app may send the message only after an edit is confirmed. Read real control bounds, text, resource ids and home-screen m

Control the project/draft state and the test content, and write every recipe for the draft it will actually start from. First check that the draft meets the field's preconditions, such as the number of clips on the target layer and special items like freezes. The default lab-phone draft has a single long clip, so split and trim checkpoints can never fire from it. Lab fixture projects exist only on

If the fixture builder fails twice with the same automation error (for example, a bottom bar item it cannot reach), retrying it unchanged will not help. Change how it reaches that tool (scroll the bar, or target the item by its content description), or move on to recipes that set up the project themselves.

If two or three recipes in a row miss the first checkpoint, replay one specific field instance in full: its device, its action sequence and its real gaps between taps. On low-end devices, slow the phone down. In one job this reproduced the crash on the first try after step-by-step recipes kept missing.

An ANR in the lab counts as a repro only if its main-thread frames match the field. Other routes (draft open, back from a tool screen) can reach the same function and give a KeyEvent ANR with a different stack. Never use a hook that fabricates the hang itself: it gives false hits that do not match the field.

To make a heavy-edit ANR, engine-thread race or lock-contention ANR fire, try undo/redo early. Tapping the edit's apply button three times did not produce a main-thread ANR. Undo/redo of the same edit did on the first try, because it replays the full engine reload back-to-back while the UI posts a blocking query. The undo control (ve_btn_undo) once failed with 'not found', so confirm its selector

Make one attempt per app process, and make sure the old process is really gone. Start every repro cycle from a fresh process with exactly the activity stack you intend. Do not call open_draft or the open-editor/slideshow step on top of a live child screen, and do not call it again inside a recipe: the stack it leaves will not reach the teardown checkpoint. Each reopen also kills the app.

The lab build's LAUNCHER is the developer test menu (com.myzesty/.MainActivity). It never touches Realm, drafts or the shipped startup path, so a plain cold launch cannot reproduce a field launch crash. Start the target Activity directly with `am start -n` (with the extras it needs, such as a draft), and make the first checkpoint that Activity being Displayed.

When a field crash repeats on every launch because of state saved on the phone, `--fresh` runs start from clean state and won't hit it. First seed the state (run the flow once, for example an asset download, then force-stop). Then damage or empty the stored value, and only then cold-start the target Activity.

Identify the installed build from facts, not guesses. The Play-installed release build also launches through com.myzesty/.MainActivity, so the launcher name does not tell you which build is installed. Use `dumpsys package com.myzesty` (versionCode plus installerPackageName=com.android.vending), and never add a setup check that aborts runs based on the launcher name. Before writing any recipes, check that the crashing statement can actually happen in the build from this checkout. Types, nullability and callers may differ from the shipped release. If the checkout has no path that produces the faulting value, stop and report that the shipped APK is needed, instead of spending a dozen lab attempts.

On this phone the wm_on_create_called event logs the activity as 'com.myzesty.MainActivity' with a dot, not 'com.myzesty/...' with a slash. Launch checkpoint regexes must accept both, e.g. `com\.myzesty[./]`, or every run fails at checkpoint 1 before the trigger.

Trust the physical phone lane, and plan for it to supply all the clean runs you need on its own. The emulator lane is unreliable. It once did not boot within 360 s and was skipped, and the APK install once failed on the first try. Recipes recorded on the phone failed every time on the emulator with 'live replay: not found' for a back-button content-desc, and the emulator has been offline.

On the Android 16 lab device, opening the sticker tool right after a draft loads kills the process about 0.4 s later with am_proc_died and no Java FATAL line. Avoid that path in recipes, or the run will log a FAIL_DIED that has nothing to do with the target crash.

Treat these harness outputs as background noise, not as a crash, repro or fix-regression signal: (1) the UNDO_WITHOUT_EDITS note ('Undo became enabled with no edits'). It appears on nearly every scenario run, including runs with no edits, engine replays and the real-taps replay, has no engine aborts and does not fail the run. (2) Repeated 'FD from fork' messages.

The repro author only sees the 'Process: com.myzesty, PID' line of a crash, so a different crash (for example, one a debug hook adds to an Activity) looks like a near-miss. Have the recipe save the whole FATAL EXCEPTION block (exception class, message, first frames), and keep hooks out of the code the crash runs through on launch.

A verify recipe must replay exactly the path that crashed. Some recipes randomize per seed (leave by back key or tap, drag direction, timing), so one crashing seed does not prove the recipe is reliable. Pin the recipe to the crashing path. A crash found by a live agent can be registered as a recipe that keeps only the navigation taps and drops the steps that actually triggered it, so check that th

Plan for the real-taps replay to run with lab shortcuts off (ZESTY_LAB=0, --record). Stop the recipe at the crash moment, and make every step before it work with real taps. Steps after the trigger that need lab shortcuts cause automation errors. They made the first verify inconclusive and made the screen-recorded repro video fail 3 times. The replay also cannot reach the editor unless the navigati

Judge verify runs strictly. A clean run counts only if it reached every field crash/trigger checkpoint and the engine log was actually captured. Some runs return no engine MsgLooper lines and cannot be judged, so check for those lines on every lane. Before you trust a PASS, check the scenario's own progress counters (for example 'speed apply 3/5') to confirm the trigger action ran its full count.

Patches (fixes and repro hooks) must apply to and compile against what the lab actually builds. Lab builds swap in the field-commit versions of the files on the crash stack. Write every diff with exact line context: against the field-commit version for crash-stack files, and against the current working tree for all other files. Never write a diff from code remembered from earlier attempts. Diffs m

Budget lab time realistically. A verify round takes about 40–45 minutes: about 1.5 minutes for the incremental arm64 build, then 2 + 6 scenario runs that each stop at about 300 s (4–5 minutes per run). A real-tap verify run takes about 3 minutes. Each natural focus run with a long clip took about 225 s, so 3 repeats cost about 11 minutes. The emulator lane takes about 40 s to boot.

A focused run (set by the flag file) runs only the registered ladder recipes. It has no engine replay, live agent or repro author to fall back on. Use it only when the registered recipe is known to reach its trigger. If the single registered step misses, do not rerun the same recipe. Clear the flag so the other repro paths can try, or register a stronger hook-based step.

The root-cause self-check rejects claims that hold for only one event: timings, error order, or errors missing from other events. Such claims cost two redo rounds of about 2 minutes each. Before submitting, check that every timing, error and step in the trigger is present in every event, and keep single-event claims out of the main story.

For use-after-teardown or null-object crashes, fix it once at the shared getter, or make the owner live for the whole process. This matters most when many JNI entry points reach the null owner. A guard that only makes the faulting function return a default value (0, empty, null, or a thrown exception) often just moves the crash. Be especially wary of a native guard that throws.

For an out-of-range index crash, unlike use-after-teardown crashes, a bounds guard at the crash site is the right fix. Reject exactly the out-of-range inputs: an invalid outer index, and an inner index past the container size. This passed the critic and code review on the first round. The reviewer checks that the guard covers every index the loop reads, so state that coverage in the fix.

For an ANR where the main thread sits in a blocking engine Get/GetResult call, do not only harden the wait. First look for a Java/Kotlin caller that polls the engine in a loop on the main thread with no exit condition or timeout.
